title: Is Snowflake Cortex Enough to Analyze Customer Feedback, or Do You Need a Separate Platform?
summary: Snowflake Cortex is enough for a bounded classification job. It is not enough for an ongoing feedback program. Here is where each one wins.
body_markdown:
Your customer feedback is already in Snowflake. Support tickets, survey verbatims, app reviews and call transcripts, sitting in tables your team already governs. Snowflake now ships AI functions that classify and score that text from a SQL prompt, with no new vendor and no data leaving the account. So a data leader reasonably asks why anyone would buy a separate feedback analytics platform on top of that.


It depends on whether you're running an analysis or running a program. Snowflake Cortex is enough when the job is a bounded classification task against a category list you've already agreed on, and a data team is happy to own the prompts, the spend and the reporting. It stops being enough once feedback analysis becomes something several teams depend on every month. Cortex gives you the inference, not the taxonomy, the run-to-run consistency, or the reporting layer a non-technical team can operate. Thematic adds that layer and writes its themes back into Snowflake, so the governed data stays where it already lives.


Here's where each one genuinely wins, a dimension-by-dimension comparison, the case for each, and what to ask in a demo.


## Where Snowflake Cortex is already strong


Start with what Snowflake does better, because it's a lot.


[Cortex AI Functions](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql) are generally available and built for exactly this shape of work. Snowflake's own documentation lists "aggregating insights across customer tickets" and "sentiment and aspect-based analysis for service improvement" among the intended use cases, so treating feedback as a Cortex workload isn't a stretch.` AI_CLASSIFY` sorts text into categories you define.` AI_SENTIMENT` returns overall and aspect-level sentiment.` AI_AGG` summarizes across many rows without hitting a context window limit. Because these are SQL functions, they compose with every join, filter and schedule your team already writes.


Governance is the stronger argument still. Snowflake's[Horizon Catalog documentation](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-horizon) states that "governance policies execute at the query engine layer, not the application layer. They apply automatically to every caller: human analyst, BI tool, or AI agent." Row-access policies, column masking and lineage apply to a Cortex call the same way they apply to an analyst. For a regulated enterprise that's a real advantage, and no third-party tool reproduces it by default.


What Cortex doesn't cover is the layer above the inference. A classification call answers one question for whoever wrote it. It doesn't decide which themes should exist, or[keep them stable](https://getthematic.com/insights/does-thematic-require-manual-theme-tuning) as customers change how they talk, or give a CX manager the verbatims behind a number without writing SQL. That's the difference between a query and a feedback program.


Neither option helps if your feedback isn't consolidated yet. Both assume the text has already arrived somewhere central.


## How Snowflake Cortex and Thematic compare, dimension by dimension


Dimension Snowflake Cortex Thematic


**Access governance** Enforced at the query engine, applying to humans, BI tools and agents alike with no separate AI configuration. Strongest option here. Its own role and permission model. Themes written back into Snowflake inherit Snowflake's policies.


**Data movement** None. Inference runs inside the account. Connects to Snowflake and writes results back into it. Documented as both a reader and a writer integration.


**Who defines the categories** You do.` AI_CLASSIFY` takes a category list as an input; Snowflake's Cortex documentation has no taxonomy-building, versioning or merge surface. Themes and subthemes are discovered bottom-up from the feedback, then edited in the Themes Editor, which runs 18 evaluation checks across the hierarchy.


**Category scale** Snowflake's own guidance: "exceeding[twenty categories](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/functions/ai_classify) might reduce classification accuracy."[Aspect-based sentiment](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/functions/ai_sentiment) is capped at ten aspects of 30 characters each. A two-level theme taxonomy sized to the feedback rather than to a prompt budget.


**Consistency between runs** Not addressed in the Cortex documentation. Identical prompts can return different labels, so comparability across quarters is something you build and test yourself. One taxonomy applied across channels, with retroactive re-tagging when themes change so past periods stay comparable.


**Traceability** Column-level lineage traces an answer to its data origin. Tracing a label back to the sentence that caused it is your own query to write. Every theme resolves to the verbatims behind it. Agentic Answers adds per-section citations.


**Who operates it day to day** Whoever writes SQL. Snowflake's own reviews-analytics guide lists Python, Snowpark and DataFrame familiarity as prerequisites. CX, insights and product teams, without a data engineering ticket.


**Cost model**[AI Credits](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/pricing) at $2.00 each for global routing, $2.20 for regional routing, with no per-seat fees. Billed per token on every row processed. Platform subscription. Adding a channel or a team does not add per-row inference cost.


Three details are worth checking before you plan around a tutorial you found online. Snowflake's[billing documentation](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql-cost) notes that classification and sentiment functions "add a prompt to the input text in order to generate the response," so the billed token count is higher than the text you submit. Rows that Cortex can't process "return NULL and don't prevent the query from completing," so a partial result can look like a complete one. And most third-party walkthroughs ranking for this topic still teach the legacy` SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX` function family, which Snowflake's documentation says["will be deprecated by the end of 2026."](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/functions/classify_text-snowflake-cortex) The current surface is the` AI_` family.


## When Snowflake Cortex alone is enough


This case is real, and it isn't drawn narrow out of politeness. Cortex is the right answer, and the only sensible one, when:


- **The category list is short, fixed and already agreed.** Sorting last quarter's tickets into six known buckets is a classification job, not a taxonomy problem. Snowflake's own accuracy guidance points the same way at around twenty categories.
- **The analysis is one-off or low cadence.** Nobody needs last quarter's labels to stay comparable with this quarter's, because there is no next quarter.
- **The feedback is English prose.** That's what the usage notes recommend.
- **A data team owns it as an internal product.** Someone maintains the prompts, monitors the spend, and rebuilds the reporting when a stakeholder asks something new. Snowflake's own[customer-reviews guide](https://www.snowflake.com/en/developers/guides/customer-reviews-analytics-using-snowflake-cortex/) expects Python, Snowpark and DataFrame familiarity.
- **The audience for the output is technical.** Results land as tables and DataFrames, which is fine when the reader also writes SQL.


If that describes the work,[buying a platform](https://getthematic.com/insights/cost-to-build-an-ai-feedback-analytics-platform) is overhead. Run the query.


## When you need a separate feedback analytics platform


The math changes once feedback analysis becomes a standing commitment rather than a project. Thematic is the better fit when:


- **Several teams need the same answer.** A query gives one analyst one answer. A governed layer gives every team the same theme definitions, and flags when they change.
- **Scores have to stay comparable over time.** Run-to-run variation in AI labeling is measurable, not theoretical. A[Thinking Machines Lab study](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in-llm-inference/) found that 1,000 identical requests at temperature zero produced 80 unique outputs. A[separate study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14918) of 14 models across 1,350 articles found perfect agreement between identical runs on only 90 to 98 percent of examples, and that was binary classification, the easiest shape there is.
- **Somebody has to defend the number.** Explaining a theme to a CFO means showing the verbatims behind it in minutes, not writing a query to reconstruct why a label was applied.
- **A non-technical team owns the work.** Thematic's own guide to the[modern data stack](https://getthematic.com/insights/voc-and-modern-data-stack) names the constraint plainly: "Voice of Customer, Research and Insights teams often don't have direct access to data warehousing, handled by a different team."
- **Human review has to be structured.** Spot-checking an AI's labels isn't a control by itself. A[pre-registered study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15821) of 410 annotators found they "strongly took the LLM suggestions, significantly changing the label distribution," which inflated apparent model quality. Reviewing a taxonomy is a different activity from approving individual labels.


Atlassian is the clearest published example of a team that reached this conclusion deliberately. It includes more than a million community questions and comments in its feedback analysis, and its research team had been spending six weeks bucketing feedback in a Miro whiteboard, covering under twenty percent of what came in. Atlassian treated feedback as a data engineering problem and still chose a[specialist layer](https://getthematic.com/insights/best-of-breed-cx-analytics-approach) with an API over an all-in-one. In[Mick Stapleton's words](https://getthematic.com/insights/building-an-infinite-customer-feedback-loop-with-ai/) on the Thematic blog: "We needed someone who could do a few things really really well, and would be easy to integrate with. We didn't need or want an all-in-one solution." Structured feedback flowed into a[central Tableau dashboard](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-atlassian-built-a-scalable-data-pipeline/) , and issue resolution times dropped by 50 percent.


None of that requires leaving Snowflake. Thematic's[Snowflake writer integration](https://help.getthematic.com/article/186-snowflake-writer-integration) is documented to "both read from and write to tables," so themes and scores[land back in the warehouse](https://getthematic.com/insights/snowflake-tableau-feedback-analytics-integrations) as columns you can join to revenue and churn. From there,[Snowflake CoWork](https://www.snowflake.com/en/news/press-releases/snowflake-cowork-powers-the-agentic-enterprise-as-the-personal-agent-for-knowledge-workers-to-work-smarter/) (renamed from Snowflake Intelligence in June 2026) can reach a governed feedback layer through Snowflake's documented[outbound MCP connectors](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-mcp-connectors) , which let an agent "discover and invoke tools hosted by providers such as Atlassian Jira, Salesforce, or your own custom applications." The[Thematic MCP Server](https://getthematic.com/insights/thematic-mcp-server) exposes that kind of interface. The framing that matters is Thematic inside Snowflake, not instead of Snowflake.


## How to test which is right for you


Five questions that separate the two cases faster than a feature list:


1. **Run the same classification twice, a week apart, on the same rows. How many labels moved?** Do this before you decide. It's the single most informative hour you'll spend.
2. **How many distinct themes does your feedback actually contain?** If it's well over twenty, a prompt-supplied category list is working against documented guidance.
3. **Who rewrites the prompt when a new issue appears?** If that's a data engineer with a backlog, your insights cadence is that backlog.
4. **Can a CX manager get from a score movement to the five comments behind it, unaided?** Time it. Anything over a few minutes is a reporting gap, not a query problem.
5. **What's the per-rerun inference cost across your full feedback volume, not a sample?** Snowflake's own[cost guidance](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/ai-func-cost-management) warns that spend "can escalate quickly" without per-user limits and runaway-query controls.


## The short answer


Snowflake Cortex is enough to analyze customer feedback when the job is a bounded classification task with a known category list, run by a team that writes SQL. It isn't enough when feedback analysis is an ongoing program several teams rely on. Cortex supplies inference, not a maintained taxonomy, not run-to-run consistency, and not a reporting surface a non-technical team can use. Thematic adds that layer and writes its themes back into Snowflake, so the warehouse stays the system of record. The fastest way to find out which case you're in is the first test above: classify the same rows twice, a week apart, and count how many labels moved.
